headings.title: Introduction and Cultural Context in Nigeria
headings.content: Hot bath practice, locally referred to in various Nigerian communities as "fashe ruwa" or steaming rituals, represents a deeply rooted traditional postpartum care method. New mothers are frequently subjected to hot water baths or vaginal steaming using herbal concoctions boiled to high temperatures. The underlying traditional philosophy assumes that excessive heat effectively cleanses the reproductive tract, expels lochia, and restores uterine tone after childbirth. While families practice this out of care and adherence to cultural norms, understanding the physiological reality of this tradition is critical for modern nursing practice.

headings.title: Physiological Effects of Excessive Heat on the Pelvis
headings.content: Exposing the female pelvic region to excessively high temperatures triggers significant local and systemic vascular responses. **Vasodilation** occurs rapidly, increasing blood flow to the skin and superficial pelvic tissues. When water temperatures exceed safe physiological limits, localized hyperthermia can induce thermal tissue damage, alter local vaginal flora balance, and impair mucosal integrity. Furthermore, sustained systemic heat exposure can cause maternal dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and transient drops in blood pressure due to peripheral pooling of blood.

headings.title: Complications and Clinical Risks
headings.content:
Engaging in extreme hot bath practices carries several direct clinical complications. 

- **Thermal Burns**: Scalding of the perineum, vulva, and thighs frequently occurs due to testing water temperature with sensitive skin or using boiling herbal infusions.
- **Ascending Infections**: Introducing hot water or unsterilized steam into the recently postpartum vagina compromises the natural barrier against bacteria.
- **Cardiovascular Instability**: Sudden orthostatic hypotension and syncopal episodes can happen when a woman stands up from a hot bath or basin.

headings.title: Impact on Fertility and Pregnancy
headings.content: Beyond the postpartum period, chronic exposure to excessive pelvic heat can negatively influence reproductive health outcomes. Elevated local temperatures can potentially disrupt normal ovarian function and alter the delicate hormonal feedback loops required for regular ovulation. In pregnant women, exposure to high hyperthermic environments—such as very hot baths or saunas—poses teratogenic risks, particularly during the critical first trimester of embryonic development, elevating the incidence of neural tube defects and spontaneous miscarriages.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Identification of Affected Women
headings.content: Effective clinical care begins with non-judgmental nursing assessment. During antenatal and postnatal booking visits, nurses must gently inquire about traditional hygiene and postpartum recovery practices without showing condemnation. Assessment should include inspecting the perineal and thigh regions for signs of erythema, blistering, or healed scald scars. Asking open-ended questions about how perineal healing is managed at home allows women to share their practices freely, enabling early identification of those engaging in hazardous thermal rituals.

headings.title: Client Education and Counseling Strategies
headings.content: Counseling regarding hot bath practices requires cultural sensitivity and evidence-based clarity. Nurses should validate the client's desire for hygiene, comfort, and healing while explaining the physiological dangers of excessive heat. Instead of forbidding the practice outright—which often drives patients to hide it—educators should offer safe alternatives, such as using warm (not hot) water for standard perineal hygiene, and ensuring herbal mixtures are cooled to body temperature before any topical contact.
